title: Chapter 1 — Loomings
paragraphs: Call me Ishmael. Some years ago — never mind how long exactly — having little or no money and nothing of interest to keep me on shore, I decided to sail around a bit and see the watery part of the world. It's my way of shaking off the blues and getting my blood flowing. Whenever I catch myself scowling; whenever it's a damp, drizzly November in my soul; whenever I find myself pausing in front of coffin shops and trailing every funeral I encounter; and especially whenever my dark moods get such a grip on me that only strong moral principle keeps me from deliberately walking into the street and methodically knocking people's hats off — then I know it's high time to get to sea. This is my substitute for a pistol and a bullet. Cato, with a philosophical flourish, throws himself on his sword; I quietly take to a ship. There's nothing surprising in this. Almost every person, at some point, feels the same pull toward the ocean that I do.

There stands your island city of Manhattan, surrounded by wharves the way Pacific isles are surrounded by coral reefs — commerce laps at it like surf. Left and right, every street leads you toward the water. The downtown tip is the Battery, where that noble seawall is washed by waves and cooled by breezes that were out of sight of land just hours before. Look at the crowds of water-gazers there.

Walk around the city on a dreamy Sunday afternoon. Go from Corlears Hook to Coenties Slip and then north by way of Whitehall. What do you see? Standing like silent sentinels all around the town are thousands upon thousands of people lost in ocean reveries. Some lean against the pilings; some sit on the pier heads; some gaze over the sides of ships from China; some perch high in the rigging, trying to get an even better view of the sea. But these are all landlocked people — weekdays they're penned up in plaster and wood, chained to counters, nailed to benches, clamped to desks. What's going on? Have all the green fields vanished? What are they doing here?

But look! Here come more crowds, heading straight for the water, seemingly ready to dive in. Strange! Nothing satisfies them but the very edge of the land; lounging in the shade of those warehouses won't do. No. They have to get as close to the water as humanly possible without falling in. And there they stand — miles of them — leagues. They come from every neighborhood, every direction — north, east, south, and west. Yet here they all converge. Do the compass needles of all those ships somehow attract them?

Consider one more thing. Say you're in the country, on some high plateau of lakes. Take almost any path you please, and nine times out of ten it will lead you down into a valley and leave you at a stream. There's something magical in it. Take the most absent-minded person alive, deep in thought, put them on their feet and set them walking — and they will inevitably lead you to water, if there's water anywhere around. If you're ever dying of thirst in the American desert, try this experiment, provided your caravan includes a philosophy professor. Yes, as everyone knows, contemplation and water are wedded forever.

And here's an artist who wants to paint the dreamiest, shadiest, most enchanting landscape in the Saco Valley. What's the essential element? Here stand his trees, each hollow-trunked as if sheltering a hermit and a crucifix; here sleeps his meadow, there rest his cattle; a sleepy trail of smoke rises from a cottage. A winding path disappears into distant woodlands, reaching toward mountain spurs bathed in blue. But though the picture seems entranced, and though the pine tree sighs leaves down upon the shepherd's head, it would all be meaningless if the shepherd's eyes weren't fixed on the magic stream before him. Visit the Prairies in June and wade knee-deep through tiger lilies for miles — what's the one thing missing? Water — not a drop to be found! If Niagara were a waterfall of sand, would you travel a thousand miles to see it? Why did the poor Tennessee poet, suddenly handed two fistfuls of silver, agonize over whether to buy the coat he desperately needed or spend the money on a trip to Rockaway Beach? Why does almost every strong, healthy young person, at some point, go crazy with the urge to go to sea? Why, on your first voyage as a passenger, did you feel that mystical vibration when told your ship was now out of sight of land? Why did the ancient Persians consider the sea holy? Why did the Greeks give it its own god, Poseidon, brother of Zeus? Surely none of this is meaningless. And deeper still is the meaning of the story of Narcissus, who plunged into the fountain and drowned because he could not grasp the tormenting, gentle image he saw there. But that same image, we see it in every river and ocean. It is the image of the ungraspable phantom of life; and this is the key to it all.

Now, when I say I go to sea whenever my eyes grow hazy and I become too aware of my own breathing, don't imagine I ever go as a passenger. Passengers need money, and a wallet is just a rag without anything in it. Besides, passengers get seasick, grow quarrelsome, don't sleep at night, and generally don't enjoy themselves much. No, I never go as a passenger; nor, though I know my way around a ship, do I ever go as a Commodore, Captain, or Cook. I leave the glory of such positions to those who want them. I personally despise all honorable, respectable labor, trials, and tribulations. I have quite enough to do just looking after myself without looking after ships, barques, brigs, and schooners. And as for going as cook — though there's considerable prestige in that, a cook being a sort of officer on board — I never much liked the idea of broiling chickens. Though once broiled, properly buttered, judiciously salted and peppered, there's no one who speaks of a broiled chicken with more respect — even reverence — than I do. It's from the ancient Egyptians' worship of broiled ibis and roasted hippopotamus that you find mummies of those creatures in their enormous bake-houses, the pyramids.

No, when I go to sea, I go as a simple sailor, right before the mast, down into the forecastle, up to the royal masthead. True, they order me around and make me jump from spar to spar like a grasshopper in a May meadow. At first, this kind of thing is unpleasant enough. It stings your pride, especially if you come from an old established family — the Van Rensselaers, or Randolphs, or Hardicanutes. And even more so if, just before dipping your hand into the tar bucket, you'd been lording it as a country schoolteacher, making the tallest boys tremble before you. The transition from schoolmaster to sailor is a sharp one, I assure you, and requires a strong dose of Seneca and the Stoics to help you grin and bear it. But even this wears off in time.

So what if some crusty old sea captain orders me to grab a broom and sweep the deck? What does that humiliation amount to, weighed on the scales of the New Testament? Do you think the archangel Gabriel thinks any less of me because I obey that old grouch? Who isn't a slave, in one way or another? Tell me that. Well, however the old captains may boss me around, thump me, and shove me, I have the satisfaction of knowing it's all fair; that everyone else gets served the same way, physically or metaphysically speaking. The universal thump gets passed around, and we should all just rub each other's shoulders and be content.

Another reason I always go as a sailor: they actually pay me for my trouble, while no one has ever paid a passenger a single penny. On the contrary, passengers have to pay. And there is all the difference in the world between paying and being paid. The act of paying is perhaps the most painful curse that Adam and Eve inflicted on us. But being paid — what compares with it? The cheerful eagerness with which a person accepts money is truly remarkable, considering how earnestly we believe money to be the root of all evil, and that no rich man can enter heaven. How gladly we consign ourselves to damnation!

Finally, I always go to sea as a sailor because of the fresh air and healthy exercise on the forecastle deck. In this world, headwinds are far more common than tailwinds (at least, if you follow the Pythagorean rule), so the Commodore on the quarterdeck mostly breathes secondhand air from the sailors up front. He thinks he breathes it first; but he doesn't. In much the same way, ordinary people lead their leaders in many things, though the leaders rarely suspect it. But why, after repeatedly going to sea as a merchant sailor, did I suddenly decide to go on a whaling voyage? That invisible police officer of Fate, who constantly watches me, secretly follows me, and steers me in mysterious ways — he can answer that better than I can. No doubt my whaling voyage was part of the grand plan of Providence, drawn up long ago. It came in as a brief interlude and solo between the larger acts. I imagine this part of the program read something like this:
“GRAND CONTESTED ELECTION FOR THE PRESIDENCY OF THE UNITED STATES.” “WHALING VOYAGE BY ONE ISHMAEL.” “BLOODY BATTLE IN AFGHANISTAN.”

Though I cannot tell exactly why those stage managers, the Fates, cast me in this shabby part of a whaling voyage, when others were assigned magnificent parts in high tragedies, short and easy parts in genteel comedies, and jolly parts in farces — though I cannot tell exactly why this was; yet, now that I recall all the circumstances, I think I can see a little into the springs and motives which, being cunningly presented to me under various disguises, induced me to set about performing the part I did. They also coaxed me into the delusion that it was a choice resulting from my own unbiased free will and discriminating judgment.

Chief among those motives was the overwhelming idea of the great whale himself. Such a gigantic, mysterious creature roused all my curiosity. Then the wild, distant seas where he rolled his enormous bulk; the nameless, unimaginable dangers of the whale hunt; these, along with all the wonders of a thousand Patagonian sights and sounds, swayed me toward my decision. Other men might not have been tempted by such things, but I am tormented by an unending itch for things far away. I love to sail forbidden seas and land on savage coasts. Not that I ignore what's good — I'm simply quick to sense a horror, and willing to keep company with it, if they'd let me. After all, it's wise to be on good terms with all the inhabitants of the place where you're staying.

For all these reasons, the whaling voyage was welcome. The great floodgates of the wonder-world swung open, and in the wild fantasies that drove me toward my purpose, two by two there floated into my deepest soul endless processions of whales — and in the middle of them all, one grand hooded phantom, like a snow hill in the air.
